---
title: "Tree-Based Methods"
---

Tree-based methods partition the feature space into regions and make
simple predictions inside each region. They are intuitive, flexible, and
often unstable enough to motivate ensembles.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain recursive binary splitting.
- Distinguish regression trees and classification trees.
- Interpret cost-complexity pruning.
- Describe why single trees can have high variance.

## Core Ideas

A tree chooses splits that reduce impurity or prediction error. The
model is easy to explain because prediction follows a sequence of
feature-based questions.

## Recursive Binary Splitting

Regression trees choose splits that reduce residual sum of squares.
Classification trees choose splits that reduce node impurity. Common
classification impurity measures are the Gini index

$$
G = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk}(1 - \hat p_{mk})
$$

and cross-entropy

$$
D = - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk}\log(\hat p_{mk}),
$$

where $\hat p_{mk}$ is the proportion of class $k$ observations in node
$m$.

## Pruning

A fully grown tree can overfit. Cost-complexity pruning chooses a
subtree by minimizing

$$
\sum_{m=1}^{|T|} \sum_{i:x_i \in R_m} (y_i - \hat y_{R_m})^2
+ \alpha |T|.
$$

The tuning parameter $\alpha$ penalizes tree size. Larger values produce
smaller trees.

```r
library(rpart)

tree <- rpart(Sales ~ ., data = ISLR::Carseats)
printcp(tree)
pruned <- prune(tree, cp = tree$cptable[which.min(tree$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"])
```

## Strengths and Limits

Trees handle interactions and nonlinearities naturally. They also
require little preprocessing. Their main weakness is instability: small
changes in the data can lead to different splits. This instability
motivates bagging, random forests, and boosting.

## Worked Example

Fit a regression tree and a classification tree. Visualize the final
tree, the feature-space partition, and the effect of pruning.

## Applied Practice

Practice by fitting a classification tree and comparing it with a
logistic regression baseline. Prune the tree using cross-validation,
then report whether the tree's interpretability and accuracy justify
using it over the linear classifier.
